npcs.name: Police Officer
dialogueTexts: As you can see, each group thinks they know what is best for the town.
Younger people and shop owners hope the government will provide funding to support local stores.
And middle-aged workers and laborers want the government to invite large companies into town.
{s}Which group do you want to speak with first?

npcs.name: Local Shop Supporter
dialogueTexts: We don’t trust large companies.
They might take the money we earn here and never spend it in town.
Local shop owners are our neighbors. They were born here, live here, and won’t leave after receiving support.
They’re also more likely to spend what they earn locally.
They’re also more likely to spend what they earn locally.
If the town government doesn’t agree, I’ll vote for a Democratic candidate and hope the town follows.

npcs.name: Large Company Supporter
dialogueTexts: How many people can one small shop hire? Two? Three?
If a large company opens a branch here, we won’t have to worry about unemployment.
The last Republican president supported plans like this. Maybe I’ll vote Republican in the next election.

npcs.name: Old Woman
dialogueTexts: {s}You walk to the edge of town and find a ruined park. An older resident stands among broken paths.
I hope they build a new park here.
Doesn’t the town feel too serious and silent these days?
Doesn’t the town feel too serious and silent these days?
Older people like us also need fresh air when we go for walks.
{s}She sighs and shakes his head.
“I’ll vote for Democrats. They care about green space and public health.
To her, this broken park is proof of neglect and unfairness. You note her values about health and shared space.

npcs.name: Worker
dialogueTexts: {s}A worker passes by and shouts back.
That would be terrible! This land was paid for by our taxes, and I still have to walk miles to work!
{y}What is going on?
There aren’t enough roads in this town. That’s why traffic is so bad.
To get to work on time, we either walk or wake up at dawn.
I’ll vote Republican in the next election. They won’t waste tax money.

npcs.name: Lobbyist
dialogueTexts: {s}A lobbyist leans forward first.
Opening a private university would bring students and professors to town.
And it wouldn’t require local tax money.
Why struggle with running something you’re not familiar with when the market can handle it?
I’m sure Republicans here would support leaving education to the market.

npcs.name: Legister
dialogueTexts: {s}A legislator exchanged glances before responding to his fellow.
Your idea makes sense. However…
The state is considering building a new public university, and our town is one possible location.
Public universities make higher education more accessible to local students.
They help keep young people here instead of only coming back for holidays.
There are disadvantages, but Democrats in this town believe it is worth the cost.

cardBattleNpcs.name: Middle Age Man
dialogueTexts: {s}A middle-aged resident stood up, his voice calm but tired.
We’ve talked about the economy for years.
Stores are closing. Jobs are disappearing.
Are we finally going to act, or just keep talking?
{s}The room murmurs as they look at you.
{s}This is no longer about detailed plans; it is about whether anything will happen now, whether you can move them from talk to action.

cardBattleNpcs.name: Local Shop Supporter
dialogueTexts: {s}A shop owner raises his hands.
Big companies promise jobs. But what happens when they leave again?
We’ve seen this before. Should we take the risk?
{s}His voice is steady, not angry, but the fear is clear. Around him, others nod.
{s}This is not about growth; it is about fear of consequences if they choose wrong again..

cardBattleNpcs.name: Kid
dialogueTexts: {s}Children and adults begin arguing at the same time.
We want a playground!
Not with our taxes!
{s}Voices overlap, sharp and confused.
So tell us—who will you support?
{s}This round is not asking for a perfect solution; it is testing whether you understand the conflict and what both sides feel is fair.

cardBattleNpcs.name: Mother
dialogueTexts: {s}A woman in the back slowly rises to speak.
My daughter will graduate next year.
A private university sounds impressive, but we’re afraid of the cost.
{s}No one interrupts; even the air feels careful.
{s}This is not a technical policy debate; it is a question about risk, debt, and regret—about what kind of future you are asking her to trust.

cardBattleNpcs.name: Old Man
dialogueTexts: {s}An older man near the aisle stands, gripping his seat.
Every option sounds risky. Moving too slowly already hurts us.
We’ve heard promises before. So tell me—what’s different this time?
{s}The room falls silent, waiting.
{s}This moment is not about statistics or fine print; it is about whether you are willing to act and let them hold you responsible.

responses: A few nods. Some support is gained.

npcs.name: Volunteer
dialogueTexts: {s}You are not on the stage, not yet. For now, you listen.
{s}A volunteer tells delegates:
Our candidate has thought this through. Education. The economy. The environment.
{s}People nod, then someone mutters, “Yes, but timing matters.”
{y}Timing matters? You mean the plan is fine, just not now?
{s}A delegate leans over.
Alex Morgan’s environmental plan adds more regulation.
Higher standards, slower change at the beginning. He’s thinking about the long run.
That’s his strength, and maybe his weakness.
{s}You think about elections, and how long patience usually lasts.
{y}It’s whether people are ready to start now.

npcs.name: Journalist
dialogueTexts: {s}Voices overlap; no one waits to finish a sentence. For now, you listen.
{s}A journalist scrolls on a tablet.
Jobs, that’s the first thing people ask about. Not next year. Now.
{s}Another reporter adds:
Everyone promises growth, but growth doesn’t feel the same to everyone.
Alex Morgan wants the government to step in more.
Public investment, support for workers. Supporters say it builds stable jobs. Critics say it’s slow and expensive.
If the economy turns before results show, voters won’t wait.
{s}You picture that gap between promise and paycheck.
{y}So it works if people can hold on. But what if they can’t?

npcs.name: Local Delegate
dialogueTexts: {s}You take a nearby seat. For now, you listen.
{s}A local delegate tells a small group.
Education always sounds safe. No one wants to be against it. But it depends on who actually gets access.
{y}What do you mean by access?
Who can afford it. Who gets in. Who has to leave home for a chance.
Alex Morgan supports more public funding—community colleges, public universities, lower costs for local students.
But it means higher public spending, and not everyone sees the benefit right away.
{y}So it’s fairer. But people still ask why they should be the ones paying.

cardBattleNpcs.name: Moderator
dialogueTexts: First question, a simple one.
When do the jobs come? Not direction. Now.
{s}The microphone goes to your opponent.
We need stable jobs, not short-lived growth. The government must step in when people need support.

cardBattleNpcs.name: Moderator
dialogueTexts: No one opposes protecting the environment.
The question is—who pays the cost?
{s}The microphone goes to your opponent.
If we don’t act now, the cost will only grow. Environmental damage doesn’t disappear.
{s}You feel hesitation in the room: people weighing risk against pain they already feel.
{s}This round is about uncertainty and who you are asking to take the hit.

cardBattleNpcs.name: Moderator
dialogueTexts: Education. Not whether it matters.
But who can actually use it?
{s}The microphone goes to your opponent.
Public education is the foundation of mobility.
{s}Some delegates think of tuition bills; others think of empty local colleges.
{s} This round is about fairness—whose door education really opens, and whose stays shut.

cardBattleNpcs.name: Moderator
dialogueTexts: Assume things go wrong, the economy slows, the budget tightens.
Who should be protected first?
{s}The microphone goes to your opponent.
The government exists to protect the vulnerable.
{s}Delegates whisper, testing each answer against their own districts.
{s}This round weighs responsibility—who you will shield and who you will ask to endure more.

cardBattleNpcs.name: Moderator
dialogueTexts: Resources are limited. Time is limited.
You have four years. What do you do first?
{s}The opponent does not rush. This round demands a choice.

responses: A few nods. Some support is gained.

what kind of candidate you are.

npcs.name: Secretary
dialogueTexts: {s}Your secretary meets you outside the stage door.
No more briefings, you’ve heard everything already— polls, interviews, crises, who’s hopeful and who’s tired.
{s}She lays six cards on the table.
These are the lines you can use tonight, not every truth, but all the space we have.
You can’t speak to everyone. Choose what they’ll remember.
{s}You look down at the cards. Each one is a way to face risk, fairness, or urgency.
{s}You won’t answer every question smoothly. Silence or vagueness would be worse.
{s}You take a breath and start arranging the cards. This will be the spine of your speech.
{s}You can feel expectation—not for details, but for direction.
{s}People have heard enough discussion, they are not asking about possibilities.
{s}They want to know: which way will you move first?
{s}Your opening words decide whether they keep listening.
{s}Choose a card.
{s}You continue.
{s}As you speak of change, the air tightens.
{s}Every national decision creates winners and losses.
{s}People are not waiting for a plan. They are waiting for a stance:
{s}When interests collide, who does the government answer to first? This is a declaration of values.
{s}Choose a card.
{s}You slow your pace.
{s}Some decisions, once made, cannot be undone.
{s}The audience knows this. They want to know:
{s}When outcomes are unclear, how do you decide whether to move forward?
{s}This part of the speech reveals how you face risk.
{s}Choose a card.
{s}You turn to society.
{s}Each citizen has a right. None coexist easily.
{s}You sense division in the room and a shared expectation:
{s}Will you acknowledge trade-offs, and stand by one set of values?
{s}This is about position.
{s}Choose a card.
{s}Your speech nears its end.
{s}Time for your last call.
{s}Four years.
{s}You cannot promise everything. You cannot avoid the question:
{s}If you must act on one category first, Where will the nation’s strength go?
{s}This is the final judgment, the one that matters most.
{s}Choose a card.

responses: A few nods. Some support is gained.

all:
Chapter 3

National Speech

The lights turn on.

You know every sentence will be interpreted.

Every
pause will be examined.

The nation is watching,

waiting
for you to speak.

The audience begins to disperse.
Conversation overtakes applause.

You
remain on the stage.

“They heard you.”
“But they chose
someone else.”

Not this time.

People stand for you.

Some applaud,
others nod in silence.

“They
listened.”
“They understood.”

You stand at the front.

The flag of the nation is now behind you.

Cameras flash.

Elected.

Now is the general election.

The country is watching.

People
do not want every detail.

They want to know your direction, your
priorities, your limits.

In this chapter,

You bring six
cards to the national stage.

They are the edges of your speech.

Each
choice shows

who you protect,

what risks you accept,

and
where the nation will move first.
